Kumbhamelā
------------------------------------------
Once in 12 years is held the biggest religious fair of the whole world, called ‘Kumbhamelā’.
As per a legend widely believed by the devout Hindus, the अमृत Kumbha or the pot of nectar that emerged out of the milky ocean during its churning, was carried away by Jayanta, the son of इन्द्र, to हेअवेन्, being hotly pursued by the असुरस् or demons. In the process of this carrying, which took him 12 days (of the gods, being equivalent to 12 human years) Jayanta is said to have dropped a little of it in four places: प्रयाग (Allahabad) (in Uttar Pradesh), Haradvāra or Hari-द्वार (now Hardwar) (in Uttaranchal), उज्जयिनी (in Madhya Pradesh) and नासिक् (in Maharashtra). That is why the कुम्भमेला fair is held, once in 12 years, in all these places by turns.
During the period of Māghamelā (a religious festival held in प्रयाग during the month of Māgha in January), hundreds of persons live on the banks of the river, practising austerities—this is called ‘Kalpavāsa’—like taking bath in the river thrice a day, living on simple ड़ोओद् or even fruits, doing a lot of जप (repetition of God’s name) and meditation and giving gifts to deserving persons.
On the special days earmarked for the bath—like the मकर सङ्क्रान्ति or Maunī Amāvāsyā—the pilgrims take a complete shave. After the ceremonial bath and offering prayers, they make gifts according to their capacities.
During the periods of कुम्भमेला thousands of साधुस् and saṁnyāsins, mendicants and religious persons of various denominations, cults and groups congregate at the sites of the melā. Apart from ceremonial processions, religious discourses, discussions, kīrtans (devotional songs) and other religio-cultural activities are also organized by them in their camps.

Kumāra
(‘the young boy’)
------------------------------------------
See SUBRAHMAṆYA.
Kumāra is also the name of a person who authored a digest of धर्मशास्त्रस् and quoted by many other authors. But nothing is known of him.
A boy below five years is called a ‘kumāra’. No cognisance is taken of any ‘sin’ or transgressions of धर्म committed by him for obvious reasons. Sometimes his parents have to undergo expiations for purifying or protecting him and themselves.

Kumārila Bhaṭṭa
------------------------------------------
Kumārila भट्ट was one of the two most important teachers and scholars who fought with the nihilistic philosophies of जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् to re-establish the glory of Vedic religion. The other teacher was शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820), his junior contemporary.
Kumārila भट्ट hailed probably from मिथिला (in Bihar) and might have lived during the period A. D. 650-700. He was a rich householder and also a great scholar. The story goes that he was defeated by a well-known Buddhist teacher, Dharmakīrti by name. After adopting बुद्धिस्म् and studying its tenets deeply under Dharmapāla, he is said to have defeated Dharmapāla himself.
As per the agreement, Dharmapāla had to commit सुइचिदे by burning himself in paddy husk set on fire.
Kumārila is also credited with victories over the Jains in the court of the king Sudhanva in Karṇāṭadeśa, in South India.
When शङ्कर came to Kumārila with a view to having a philosophical disputation, he was actually burning himself as an expiation for the sin of cheating his Buddhist गुरु. As per his direction, शङ्कर is said to have gone to मण्डन मिश्र for the same.
Kumārila was a very great scholar. He has written, in the vārttika form (explanatory notes in verses), a detailed commentary on the Śābarabhāṣya of the Mīmāṁsāsūtras of जैमिनि. They are in three parts known as Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā. Other works attributed to him by certain later writers—such as Bṛhatṭīkā and Madhyamaṭīkā—are not available now.
Prabhākara, मण्डन मिश्र and Umbeka (or भवभूति) were his chief disciples.

Kumbhakoṇam
------------------------------------------
The town of कुम्भकोणम् is one of the oldest centres of Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे in South India. It is situated at a distance of 70 kms. (43 miles) to the south-west of another famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे, चिदम्बरम् (in Tamil Nadu). The rivers कावेरी and Arasalar flow on the two sides of the town.
The Amṛtakumbha (pot containing nectar) established by ब्रह्मा, the creator, at the instance of शिव, is said to have stopped here, after being carried by the waters of प्रलय (destruction of the world). Hence the name कुम्भकोणम्.
This town contains many ancient temples. There are twelve of शिव, four of विष्णु and one of ब्रह्मा (which is extremely rare).
The temple of Sāraṅgapāṇi (Viṣṇu) is the most imposing of all the temples. Its central shrine is probably the oldest part of the complex since eight of the twelve आऌवार्स् have sung its praise. Additions were made by the Nāyak kings during the period A. D. 1300-1700. Its gopuram (tower) is 44 metres (146 feet) high and has 12 storeys. There are numerous ornamental figures.
Two main entrances lead to the central shrine. The southern entrance is used during the दक्षिणायन period (period of the southern solstice, July to January) and the northern entrance during the उत्तरायण period (period of northern solstice, january to July).
The shrine of Komalavallī (Lakṣmī, consort of विष्णु) is in the northern part of the temple.
There is a puṣkaraṇī (temple tank) also, next to the temple, meant for bathing by the devotees before they enter. The annual teppotsava (floating festival) is also held here in the month of Māśi (in March).
The पूजा (worship) and allied rituals are done according to the Pāñcarātra Āgamas.
There are two big rathas (temple chariots) made of wood with elaborate carvings. There is, in addition, one made of silver used on special occasions.
The Kumbheśvara temple also is a big one and is located in the centre of the town. Its main gopuram is 38 metres (128 feet) high and has many intricately carved sculptures on it. The temple can boast of quite a few silver vāhanas (palanquins) used to carry the various deities during festival days.
There is another temple of Śiva—known as Nāgeśvara शिव temple—which contains a shrine for सूर्य (the Sun-god) also. The rays of the sun enter the inner sanctum through the openings in the gopuram three times a year and fall right on the शिवलिङ्ग! This is considered as the worship of शिव by सूर्य himself.
The Rāmasvāmi temple built probably in the 16th century has the images of राम’s brothers also apart from that of सीता. There are sculptures on the pillars and murals on the walls depicting scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa.
Some of the other Vaiṣṇavite temples of कुम्भकोणम् are: Cakrapāṇi temple; Varāha temple; Gopālasvāmi temple; वरदराज temple and Vedanārāyaṇa temple.
Another important place for the pilgrims in कुम्भकोणम् is the Kanyātīrtha, more commonly known as the Mahāmāgham tank. It is a huge lake spread over an area of 20 acres (8 hectares). There are 16 towers with maṇḍapas (small halls) all-round this tank. Once in 12 years, on the pūrṇimā (full-मोओन्) day of the month of Māgha (in February) when गुरु (Jupiter) is in Siṁha (Leo) and चन्द्र (Moon) is in the Makha नक्षत्र, a very big bathing festival is held here. This is called Mahāmākham or Mahāmāgham. All the sacred rivers are supposed to be present in the water on this day.
There is also an ancient मठ (or monastery belonging to the Advaita tradition)—the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi Pīṭham—in कुम्भकोणम् existing since A. D. 1743.

Kumbhakarṇa
(‘one whose ears were like a pot’)
------------------------------------------
See RĀMĀYAṆA.

Kumbhābhiṣeka
(‘pouring [water] from a [consecrated] pot’)
------------------------------------------
Kumbhābhiṣeka is the ceremonial act of pouring the water from a duly consecrated pot, on to the pinial (kalaśa) of a Hindu temple.
Generally, several pots with water and certain prescribed materials, are established inside the sanctum. After a simple worship, the presence of the chief deity of the temple is invoked into these pots. Either all the pots or one bigger pot containing a little of the water of every pot, is carried to the top of the temple tower and emptied over the pinial. This is done from a specially built platform of wooden poles so that one need not step upon the tower.
By this act, the presence of the main deity is transferred to the pinial also.
Any one going at a distant place, unable to visit the temple, can get the merit of seeing the main deity just by bowing down to the consecrated pinial.

Kumāra-Vyāsa
(‘the young or junior व्यास’)
------------------------------------------
The Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata have influenced the Hindu psyche to such an extent over the last two millennia that works in many vernaculars, either summarising them or imitating them or adopting them as the basis, have been composed. The most well-known Mahābhārata in the Kannada language is the Karṇāṭa-bhārata-kathāmañjarī, more popularly known as Kumāra व्यास Bhārata or Gadugina Bhārata.
The author of this work, Nāraṇappa, lived most probably during the period A. D. 1350 to 1425. He belonged to a village near Gadag in Northern Karnataka and was a devotee of Vīranārāyaṇa, the deity of the chief temple there. He was probably a vaiṣṇava of the भागवत school. His work is a poetical composition in the well-known metre called ‘bhāminīṣaṭpadī’. It is in ten parvas or books or sections and covers the entire story of the Mahābhārata. Śrī कृष्ण is the chief hero in this work. Its literary quality has been highly eulogised.
Airāvata is another poetical work attributed to him. It deals with the heroic exploits of अर्जुन, the Pāṇḍava hero.
